title: Design concept and phase transformation study of advanced bainitic-austenitic medium-Mn steel
abstract: Abstract The isothermal heat treatment processing routes are designed for a novel 0.17 C-3.1Mn-1Si-0.55Al-0.22Mo-0.034Ti-0.073 V steel, aiming to obtain a homogeneous fine lath-type microstructure consisting of bainitic ferrite and retained austenite (RA). The phase transformation of the investigated steel is studied employing high-resolution dilatometry. Isothermal heat treatment cycles below and above the martensite start (M s ) temperature are performed to analyse the kinetics of bainitic transformation as well as the thermal stability of retained austenite. Microstructural characterization is carried out using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The quantitative analysis of individual microstructural constituents is performed based on the differences in diffraction pattern quality using the deep learning (DL) evaluation method and compared with the results of X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements. The thickness of bainitic ferrite laths (BFL) is predicted using an approach integrating thermodynamic and kinetic parameters, achieving overall good agreement with the experimental observations. It is demonstrated that the isothermal holding temperature of 400 °C is the most beneficial material state in terms of the kinetics of bainitic transformation and stabilization of RA. The microstructure is consisted of fine BFLs with a mean thickness of 124 nm, the lath-type RA (10.3 vol%), and a small fraction of martensitic-austenitic islands.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The production of high-quality forgings intended for the automotive and machine industry is a challenge for manufacturers due to various technological difficulties, such as obtaining the intended geometry while ensuring high mechanical properties and maintaining low production costs 1  and, since the last years, achieving minimum environmental impacts 2 , 3 . Advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) with high (15–30 wt%) and medium (3–12 wt%) manganese contents have received much attention during the last decade 4 ,  5 – 6 . However, the 2nd generation of AHSS (high manganese steels) still lacks industrial application, mostly as the high manganese content causes numerous technological difficulties during production 7 , 8 . Therefore, the medium-Mn steels with comparably reduced Mn content belonging to the newest 3rd generation of AHSS are currently the most promising candidates for future automotive steel grades. Bainitic concepts containing retained austenite (RA) are of specific interest, as the transformation of RA to martensite during various loading conditions 9  is beneficial for increasing toughness and ductility 10 . Furthermore, reducing the heat treatment of forgings steels from a standard quenching and tempering treatment to a process that uses the residual heat from the forging process, can lead to significant reductions of the CO 2 -emissions (global warming potential) 2 , 11 . The combination of appropriately selected thermomechanical processing conditions and the use of controlled cooling enables the production of a bainitic microstructure with a fine lath-type RA, which is crucial for obtaining high strength and ductility as well as high cracking resistance 12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 . During crack propagation, RA effectively prevents the growth of cracks by its transformation to martensite, which introduces a volume expansion in the vicinity of the crack tip, leading to a halt of the propagation and potentially to crack closure 16 , 17 .

In order to produce economical forgings showing high cracking resistance as well as fatigue and impact strength, the conditions of heat treatment and thermomechanical processing must be designed and optimized in accordance with the specific application. The processing of steel intended for bainitic-austenitic forgings usually includes austenitization, forging with consecutive controlled cooling to the bainitic transformation range, followed by isothermal holding. During the isothermal holding, 10–15 vol% of RA are stabilized 18 , 19 ; phase fraction and stability of the RA are depended mostly on the time and temperature of the isothermal holding 20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 . In 24  the authors investigated a low-Mn steel 0.33 C-2.23(Mn + Cr)-1.07%Si with a microstructure composed of carbide-free bainite and RA, intended for components used in railway infrastructure. The investigations were performed for different variants of the isothermal holding temperature in a range from 350 °C to 480 °C. They observed a tendency that lowering the isothermal holding temperature resulted in an increase in the carbon content in austenite, which led to the stabilization of this phase and, as a result, to an increase in its volume fraction. A similar relationship was reported by Meng et al. 25  for steel 0.28 C-2.14Mn-0.82Si-1.62Cr-0.33Ni-0.22Mo.

The majority of studies focus on the design of Mn steels for flat products, describing high strength and ductility in this steel class, as well as the TRIP (transformation-induced-plasticity) effect 26 ,  27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33 . However, the medium-Mn bainitic-austenitic steels have not yet been considered for the use in forgings, which highlights the originality of this research field. In the present study, the phase transformation of a novel 0.17 C-3.1Mn-1Si-0.55Al-0.22Mo-0.034Ti-0.073 V steel was investigated to design and optimize the time-temperature parameters for further thermomechanical processing of bainitic-austenitic forgings. The microstructural changes during continuous cooling and isothermal holding at the bainitic region in a temperature range from 360 °C to 440 °C were monitored using high resolution dilatometry. The final microstructures were qualitatively and quantitatively assessed using modelling and experimental approaches.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The ingot with a square cross-section of 100 mm and weight of approximately 100 kg was produced in a VSG 100 S vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere. The ingot was hot-rolled in 3 passes into a flat bar with a thickness of 22 mm. The hot rolling process was carried out in the temperature range of 1200 –900 °C on the LPS/B semi-industrial line located at Łukasiewicz Research Network - Upper Silesian Institute of Technology in Gliwice, Poland. The ingot was austenitized for 2 h at 1200 °C before hot rolling. Chemical analyses of the C, Mn, Si, Al, Mo, Ti and V contents in steel were performed using the spark excited optical emission spectrometry. The chemical composition of the investigated steel is shown in Table  1 . In order to maintain good machinability of the steel, the amount of carbon added into the steel was reduced to 0.17% 34 . The addition of ~ 3 wt% manganese reduces the M s  temperature of steel 35 . Silicon and aluminum were added in order to reduce the amount of cementite formed during bainitic transformation 36 . Moreover, Al addition introduced into the steel accelerates the kinetics of the bainitic transformation, which is beneficial from the technological point of view 6 , 37 . The Mo addition was added to improve hardenability, toughness and hot ductility. Ti and V were added to stabilize the austenite grain size during the heat treatments 38 .
Table 1 Chemical composition of investigated steel in wt%. C Mn Si Al Mo Ti V Fe 0.17 3.10 1.00 0.55 0.22 0.034 0.073 bal.

The phase transformation kinetics was studied using a high-resolution BÄHR DIL 805 A/D dilatometer. Samples with a dimension of ⌀ 5 mm x 10 mm were used for the tests. Induction heating was applied; the heat treatments were carried out in a helium atmosphere. The temperature was controlled using an S-type thermocouple welded to the sample surface. Al 2 O 3  anvils and push-rods were used during experiments. Dilatometric data were analyzed using the technique of applying a tangent to the dilatation curve near the start and finish of the transformation described in ASTM A1033-04 39 . The moment at which the elongation of the sample started to increase during isothermal holding was considered as the beginning of the bainitic transformation.

In order to create the DCCT and DTTT diagrams, samples were initially heated at a rate of 3 °C/s to a temperature of 1100 °C and austenitized for 300 s. Then, samples were cooled to a temperature of 900 °C and deformed with a deformation degree of 50% (from length of 10 mm to final 5 mm) at a rate of 10s -1  which corresponds to the industrial process of die forging 40 , 41 . The deformation parameters were applied to reflect the typical final forging conditions 42 . In order to analyze the kinetics of phase transformations during continuous cooling, samples were cooled to room temperature at a cooling rate range from 60 °C/s to 0.05 °C/s (DCCT diagram). The holding time for each isothermal treatment to determine the DTTT diagrams were selected to be 3 h. After deformation, samples were cooled to the various isothermal holding temperatures from 380 °C to 520 °C at a rate of 60 °C/s. After isothermal holding, samples were cooled to room temperature at a rate of 1 °C/s. Based on the obtained DTTT diagrams, the initial temperature variants of isothermal holding at the bainitic region were selected.

The samples used to investigate the influence of different isothermal holding temperatures at the bainitic transformation range on the microstructure of investigated steel were initially heated to the austenitizing temperature of 1100 °C at a rate of 10 °C/s to, held at this temperature for 300 s and cooled to the deformation temperature of 900 °C. The samples were deformed with a 50% deformation degree and then they were cooled with a cooling rate of 1 °C/s to the different isothermal holding temperatures in a range of 440 –360 °C (Fig.  1 ).
Fig. 1 Scheme of temperature variants of isothermal holding at the bainitic region.

The samples after dilatometric measurements were prepared for further metallographic investigations. The undeformed samples were cut in half and embedded in a resin. Due to the barrel-shaped geometry of the samples resulting from deformation, longitudinal sectioning at one-third of the diameter was performed to ensure that the examined cross-section reflected a representative deformation state for subsequent microstructural characterization 43 . Then they were ground using SiC paper up to 1200 grid, polished with 6, 3 and 1 μm diamond, respectively. In order to investigate the microstructure under light optical microscope (LOM) and scanning electron microscope (SEM), the samples were etched with 3% Nital solution after the last polishing step. For the electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) measurements, an additional polishing was conducted using oxide polishing suspension (OPS), following the last polishing step of 1 μm. The OPS polishing was employed manually for 20 min, without applying excessive force. The specimen was rotated 90° every two and a half minutes to ensure homogeneous polishing. At the end of the polishing process, the surface of the specimens was cleaned with water and alcohol to guarantee and protect the surface quality. The microstructures were observed using the Zeiss Observer Z1m light microscope and the Zeiss Supra 25 scanning electron microscope working at secondary electrons (SE) mode. Measurements were carried out using a working distance of 14 mm and an accelerating voltage of 20 kV. The EBSD measurements were performed using the Zeiss Sigma SEM field-emission gun. The NordlysNano detector was used for the EBSD measurements with a 75 μm aperture, an accelerating voltage of 20 kV, a working distance of 17 mm and a step size of 50 nm. For the EBSD post-processing, AZtecCrystal software from Oxford Instruments and MTEX Toolbox of MATLAB were used.

The morphology of RA and mean size of bainitic ferrite laths (BFL) at different isothermal holding temperatures of 360 °C, 400 °C and 440 °C were assessed using S/TEM images obtained in transmission electron microscope (TEM) Titan 80–300, FEI working at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV. The TEM lamellae obtained by focused ion beam (FIB) milling was used. The mean size of bainitic laths at different isothermal holding temperatures was assessed based on 30 measurements for each variant.
Mn, Al – concentration of manganese and aluminium (wt%) in the austenite.

The hardness measurements were performed using the Vickers method at a load of 100 kgf (Future-Tech FM-700 Vickers hardness tester) in accordance with the PN-EN ISO 6507-1 standard. Ten measurements were performed for each variant.

sections.heading: Phase transformation kinetics during continuous cooling and isothermal holding
paragraphs: The DCCT diagrams were determined to characterize the hardenability of investigated steel, because after a final forging step they should be cooled to an isothermal holding temperature in the bainitic region without formation of ferrite or pearlite. The plastic deformation applied before cooling accelerates the kinetics of ferritic, pearlitic and bainitic transformation, thus the DCCT diagram provides information crucial for designing the parameters of thermomechanical processing. The DCCT (Fig.  2 a) and DTTT (Fig.  2 b) diagrams were analyzed to identify the optimal heat treatment parameters that facilitate the formation of a bainitic–austenitic microstructure. The DCCT diagram was developed to determine the critical cooling rate required to suppress the formation of transformation products other than martensite. The DTTT diagram was developed to define the time–temperature conditions of isothermal holding that enable the stabilization of about 8–15 vol% of RA. In order to develop the DCCT diagram, several thermal cycles at various continuous cooling rates were performed (Fig.  2 a). Dilatometry allows to determine the critical temperatures: A c1  and A c3 , which were 719 °C and 930 °C, respectively 52 . The investigated steel shows relatively high hardenability. The fully martensitic microstructures were observed in a wide range of cooling rates from 60 °C/s (Fig.  3 a) to 5 °C/s (Fig.  3 b). The fully bainitic microstructure was observed only at the lowest cooling rates of 0.1 °C/s and 0.05 °C/s (Fig.  3 c). The M s  temperature increases with decreasing cooling rate from 60 °C/s (M s  = 354 °C) to 0.5 °C/s (M s  = 386 °C). This phenomenon is most likely related to the recrystallization, which is more advanced in slowly cooled alloys 53 . The results of dilatometric tests were confirmed by results of hardness measurements (Fig.  2 c). It was observed that as the cooling rate decreased, the hardness of the investigated steel gradually decreased. The decrease from 473HV1 to 448HV1 with decreasing the cooling rate to 5 °C/s was related to the in-situ tempering effect of martensite, which is more advanced at lower cooling rates. The further decrease in hardness of samples cooled in a range of 1–0.05 °C/s was related to an increase in the amount of bainitic ferrite formed in the microstructure. The sample showing fully bainitic microstructure formed during cooling at a rate of 0.05 °C/s (Fig.  3 c) has the lowest hardness ~ 377HV1.

Fig. 2 Determined DCCT ( a ) and DTTT ( b ) diagrams together with their corresponding hardness measurements ( c  and  d , respectively) as well as the change in M s -temperature after isothermal holding (also d).

Fig. 3 Exemplary microstructures obtained by continuous cooling ( a – c ) and isothermal holding ( d – f ). The microstructures were found to be either completely martensitic (cf. a, b, d) or bainitic (cf. c and d), only e displays a mixed microstructure consisting of a bainitic matrix with minor shares of martensite as indicated.

The DTTT diagram (Fig.  2 b) was determined during the 3-hours isothermal holding step performed in a temperature range from 380 °C to 520 °C up to completion of the bainitic transformation. This study was conducted to select the most optimal isothermal holding temperatures in the bainitic transformation field for further experiments aimed at optimizing the thermal stability of RA. During the 3-hour isothermal holding only bainitic and martensitic transformations were registered. The obtained results also showed that the bainitic transformation took place in a temperature range from 500 °C to 380 °C. At a temperature of 380 °C the bainitic transformation started immediately (no incubation time) because the isothermal holding was performed slightly below the M s  temperature (M s  = 385 °C). The completion of the bainitic transformation also occurred fast at this temperature (690s). It is caused by the formation of prior martensite in the microstructure 54 . For the range of isothermal holding temperatures above the M s  temperature, the bainitic transformation occurred the fastest at 420 °C (incubation time about 2s). The completion of the bainitic transformation at this temperature took place after 1044s. As a result of the increased Mn content, formation of ferrite and pearlite were not observed 34 , 55 . At the same time, Mn slows down the bainitic transformation and delays its field to longer times 35 . However, this effect is masked by the Al addition, which accelerates the kinetics of bainitic transformation. Such tendency was also observed by Tian et al. 56  for a steel containing 2 wt% of Mn and 0.5 wt% of Al.

Obtained results (Fig.  2 d) showed that the isothermal holding temperature strongly influences the M s  temperature of steel. It was noted that as the temperature of isothermal holding decreases, the M s  temperature also decreases. The M s  temperature drops from approximately 382 °C after isothermal holding at 520 °C to about 250 °C after isothermal holding at 380 °C. Due to the high M s  temperature, the microstructure of steel after isothermal holding at 520 °C (Fig.  3 f) is fully martensitic and RA was not observed (Table  2 ). The amount of bainitic ferrite in the microstructure increased with decreasing isothermal holding temperature (Fig.  3 d and e ). Morawiec et al. 54  observed a similar effect, whereby an increase in the isothermal holding temperature within the bainitic transformation range led to a reduced fraction of bainite in the microstructure of the 0.17 C-3.3Mn-1.6Al-0.23Mo-0.22Si steel. This led to a lower carbon enrichment and corresponding lower thermal stability of austenite. The same temperature-related trend was noted for RA (Table  2 ). The highest fraction of RA (about 10 vol%) was noted for a sample isothermally treated at the lowest temperature of 380 °C. The RA was thermally stable for the isothermal holding temperature range from 420 °C to 380 °C and the fraction of RA in the microstructure was in a range of 8–10 vol%. The results of hardness measurements (Fig.  2 d) are consistent with microstructure observations (Fig.  3 d-f) and results of dilatometric measurements (Fig.  2 b). The hardness of the steel decreased from 464HV1 at a temperature of 520 °C to 384HV1 after isothermal holding at 380 °C. It is related to the decrease in the fraction of hard martensite in the microstructure in favor of softer bainitic ferrite and ductile RA. Obtained results showed that isothermal holding temperatures in a range of 420 –380 °C are the most promising in terms of stabilizing RA.

For the latter, corresponding carbon concentration in the RA as well as the hardness are displayed as well. sections.heading: Influence of isothermal holding temperatures on the thermal stability of retained austenite
paragraphs: The heat treatment trials enabling to obtain microstructures composed of bainitic ferrite and RA were performed using dilatometry. The dilatometric curves obtained during cooling from deformation temperature 900 °C to the different isothermal holding temperatures in a range of 360–440 °C are shown in Fig.  4 a.

Fig. 4 Dilatometric curves recorded during: ( a ) cooling from deformation temperature 900 °C to the different isothermal holding temperatures, ( b ) isothermal holding at different temperatures, ( c ) relative change in samples’ length and ( d ) derivate relative change in samples’ length during isothermal holding.

A small increase in relative change in length of samples during cooling from deformation temperature 900 °C to the isothermal holding temperatures of 360 °C and 380 °C was detected. An increase is the sample volume indicates the transformation of austenite into martensite. This is due to the fact that M s  temperature of steel is higher (M s  = 385 °C, Fig.  2 a) than isothermal holding temperatures of 360 °C and 380 °C. The martensitic transformation was not detected during cooling to the isothermal holding temperatures in a range of 400–440 °C. The isothermal holdings at the bainitic field were carried out in a temperature range from 440 °C to 360 °C. The obtained dilatometric curves are shown in Fig.  4 . At the isothermal temperatures of 360 °C and 380 °C the bainitic transformation started immediately after the initiation of isothermal holding (Fig.  4 b). At the same time, the lowest relative change in sample length (RCL) was observed, approximately 0.05% and 0.1% for isothermal holding at temperatures of 360 °C and 380 °C, respectively. This means that for these temperature variants some small amount of bainite was formed. The DRCL (derivate relative change in samples length) is a reflection of the actual RLC (Fig.  4 d), enabling the assessment of the bainitic transformation rate 57 . Before reaching 600s both curves are flat, which means that in both cases the bainitic transformation is completed. A close correlation between temperature and the nucleation rate was observed. Isothermal holding temperatures of 360 °C and 380 °C are below the M s  temperature (M s  = 385 °C, Fig.  2 a) and therefore some fraction of martensite was formed (Fig.  4 a), which reduces the incubation time and accelerates the bainitic transformation 53 , 58 . The prior martensite causes localized deformation in the austenite leading to an increase in its dislocation density, thus lower energy is needed for bainite nucleation 59 . Consequently, a greater number of nucleation sites is present in the microstructure affecting both the incubation period and the overall kinetics of the bainitic transformation 60 . For the remaining temperature variants of isothermal holding above the M s  temperature, the incubation time was observed.

For the sample isothermally treated at 400 °C the strongest dilatometric signal was recorded, which means that the isothermal holding at this temperature allows to obtain the largest fraction of bainite. The obtained results show that at this temperature, the incubation time of bainitic transformation is approximately 20s and after reaching 600s, an increase in the RCL of the sample stops at approximately 0.28% (plateau is reached), which is interpreted as the completion of the bainitic transformation.

The isothermal heat treatment at the highest temperatures of 420 °C and 440 °C resulted in the incubation time of bainitic transformation: 90s and 40s, respectively. The slope of the dilatometric curve after isothermal holding at 420 °C is higher compared to the results obtained at 440 °C, which is attributed to the faster kinetics of bainitic transformation. However, for both isothermal holding temperatures of 420 °C and 440 °C, the relative change in the length of samples increases continuously after 600s, which indicates the incomplete bainitic transformation phenomenon. Such effect is related to the differences in driving force of the bainitic transformation, which tends to increase with decreasing isothermal holding temperature 58 . The higher driving force of the bainitic transformation allows to obtain a larger fraction of bainite in the microstructure. At the isothermal holding temperatures below M s  some fraction of prior martensite was formed, which causes the decrease in a fraction of bainite 54 .

After completing the isothermal holding process for 600 s, the samples were cooled to the room temperature. The analysis of the dilatometric curves during final cooling from the isothermal holding temperature to the room temperature allows to assess the thermal stability of austenite. An increase of the sample length related to the martensitic transformation was not observed in samples isothermally held at 360 °C and 380 °C. The temperatures of 360 °C and 380 °C are below the M s  temperature and therefore some fraction of austenite transformed into martensite during the isothermal holding step and the remaining fraction stayed stable during final cooling. The remaining fraction of RA was enriched in carbon diffusing from the supersaturated martensite and BFL and finally stabilized to the room temperature. The dilatometric curve of the sample isothermally held at 400 °C shows a small signal from the martensitic transformation. It indicates that a small fraction of undesired fresh martensite (FM) was formed during cooling.

During cooling to the room temperature from isothermal holding temperatures of 440 °C and 420 °C higher fraction of FM was formed when compare to the sample isothermally held at 400 °C, as the pronounced deviation in RCL of the sample was recorded (Fig.  4 c). It was also observed that, for the sample subjected to isothermal heat treatment at the highest temperature (440 °C), the dilatometric response was the strongest and the highest M s  temperature (~ 361 °C) was recorded. It indicates that the highest fraction of FM was formed in the microstructure. The sample isothermally treated at 420 °C showed the lower M s  temperature ~ 344 °C than the sample held at 440 °C. The decrease in isothermal holding temperature from 440 °C to 420 °C effectively reduced the M s  temperature due to increased carbon enrichment in the austenite. This enrichment results from carbon partitioning from supersaturated bainitic ferrite into the austenite during the transformation, leading to reduce the M s  temperature. The decrease in bainitic transformation temperature enhances the thermodynamic driving force for bainite formation. As a result, an increased amount of carbon is partitioned into the surrounding austenite, leading to an increase in carbon concentration and subsequently reducing the martensite start M s  temperature. The obtained results show that decreasing the isothermal holding temperature from 440 °C to 400 °C has a positive effect on the stability of RA.

sections.heading: Influence of isothermal holding temperatures on the microstructure evolution
paragraphs: The bainitic transformation temperature influences the amount and morphology of bainitic ferrite, as well as the final fraction of RA in the microstructure of investigated steel. Figure  5  shows the microstructures of samples isothermally held at 360 °C, 400 °C and 420 °C during 600s. The fine, lath-type microstructures were observed for all investigated isothermal holding temperatures. The effective reduction of cementite precipitation is caused by the Si and Al additions 61 . It is beneficial because a larger content of carbon is available in the solid solution to enrich RA and to stabilize this phase to the room temperature. Due to microadditions of Ti and V, which can form TiC, TiN, VN, V(C, N) and more complex compounds 38 , the growth of austenite grains during austenitization was limited and therefore the fine lath-type microstructures were obtained.

The sample isothermally treated at 360 °C shows the microstructure composed of bainitic ferrite and lath-type RA (Fig.  5 a, b). Only very small fraction of FM was observed in the microstructure. No martensite transformation was noted in the dilatometric curve (Fig.  4 c) during final cooling to the room temperature, which can be related to the heterogeneous distribution of Mn within the microstructure, which is often observed in medium-Mn steels 57 , 62 . Locally, the M s  temperature of steel can be higher due to the formation of Mn-poor and Mn-rich regions 63 . Some fraction of MA (martensitic-austenitic) constituents was formed at 360 °C (Fig.  5 a). RA stayed stable in the outer areas of MA islands, while the inner area transformed into martensite. The MA constituents identified in the sample subjected to isothermal heat treatment at 360 °C may show tempering effects, since their formation could occur during isothermal holding below the M s  temperature (M s  = 385 °C). The presence of MA constituents was also revealed using TEM (Fig.  6 a, b). The presence of RA was confirmed by selected area diffraction (Fig .6c). Two types of bainitic ferrite were observed in the microstructure of the sample heat treated at 360 °C (Fig.  5 a, b). The bainitic ferrite in a form of thin laths, which is dominant and some fraction of wider laths classified as coalesced bainite. Bhadeshia et al. 64  observed the formation of coalesced bainite in C-Mn-Si type steels. The coalesced bainite forms as a result of decomposition of austenite located near its grain boundaries. This process results in an increase in bainite lath thickness due to merging of individual thin laths. Such effect is observed at relatively low transformation temperatures (below 400 °C) at which the driving force for bainitic transformation is sufficiently high 65 . The early stage of coalesced bainite formation is shown in Fig. 10a and b. The RA laths are decomposed only partially and the formation of coalesced bainite is not finished. As a result of coalesced bainite formation carbon is trapped in bainitic ferrite and it can further precipitate or partition into RA located near α/γ interface 64 .

Fig. 5 Microstructures of investigated steel after isothermal holding at 360 °C ( a ,  b ), 400 °C ( c ,  d ) and 420 °C ( e ,  f ) (CB – coalesced bainite, FM – fresh martensite, MA – martensitic-austenitic islands, RA – retained austenite).

The fine lath-type bainitic-austenitic microstructure was observed in a sample after isothermal holding at 400 °C (Fig.  5 c, d). RA showing the beneficial lath-type morphology is located between BFL. The thickness of RA laths presented on TEM images (Fig.  6 d, e) does not exceed ~ 180 nm. The presence of RA was confirmed by selected area diffraction (Fig.  6 f). The lath-type RA shows higher mechanical stability than blocky RA 66  and contributes to an increase in toughness and fatigue strength of steel, which are crucial properties for forgings 67 , 68 . A small fraction of martensitic-austenitic (MA) constituents was observed in the microstructure after isothermal holding at 400 °C (Fig.  5 c). No martensitic transformation was noted during final cooling to the room temperature (Fig.  4 c), which indicates its small amount formed just as a result of Mn segregation 56 , 62 .

An increase in the isothermal holding temperature to 420 °C resulted in an increase in the fraction of undesired FM (marked with dashed blue lines) identified in the microstructure (Fig.  5 e, f). The FM observed in samples isothermally heat treated at 400 °C (Fig.  5 e) and 420 °C (Fig.  5 f) was formed as a result of martensitic transformation of block-type low-stable austenite during cooling to the room temperature. Besides of the lath-type RA observed in the SEM image (Fig.  5 e, f), the presence of small blocky-type RA was revealed using TEM (Fig.  6 g, h). FM shows a high carbon content and resulting brittleness accelerating the initiation and propagation of microcracks during service conditions of forgings. In the study 69 , authors reported that FM areas exhibit high hardness and brittleness, which limits their ability to accommodate plastic deformation. Therefore, the interfaces between FM and austenite may act as preferential sites for the nucleation of local damage, such as void formation or crack initiation. The negative influence of FM on the toughness of steel containing 2.2 wt% of Mn was reported by Li et al. 70 . They observed that an increase in the amount of FM in the microstructure of steel from 3.2 to 9.3% resulted in the decrease in toughness from 102 J/cm 2  to 42 J/cm 2 .

Fig. 6 TEM images of investigated steel after isothermal holding at different temperatures: ( a ) 360 °C bright field, ( b ) corresponding dark field of RA and ( c ) SAD pattern of RA, ( d ) 400 °C bright field, ( e ) corresponding dark field of RA and ( f ) SAD pattern of RA, ( g ) 440 °C bright field, (h) corresponding dark field of RA and martensite and (i) SAD pattern of RA and (j) SAD pattern of martensite.

In order to further characterize the microstructure of investigated steel after isothermal holdings at 360 °C, 400 °C and 420 °C, the EBSD measurements were performed. The distinction (Fig.  7 a-f) and quantitative analysis (Fig.  7 g-i) of individual microstructural constituents were performed based on the differences in diffraction pattern quality using the deep learning (DL) evaluation method 61 , 67 . The dark areas with a low pattern quality characterized by the low value of the IQ parameter are associated with FM formed during final cooling to the room temperature (Fig.  7 a-c). The martensitic transformation of unstable austenite is related to the formation of martensite of higher dislocation density than in tempered martensite or bainite showing higher IQ values 69 . The highest fraction (~ 15.3%) of FM (marked in yellow) was formed in a sample isothermally held at 420 °C (Fig.  7 i), whereas the lowest fraction was noted in a sample heat treated at 400 °C (~ 8.9%) - Fig.  7 h. The observed tendency is consistent with the results of dilatometric response (Fig.  4 a). The FM formed as a result of martensitic transformation of blocky-type RA located mainly at the prior austenite grains boundaries (Fig.  7 d-f).

Fig. 7 Image quality maps of investigated steel after isothermal holding at 360 °C ( a ), 400 °C ( b ), 420 °C ( c ); image quality maps combined with phase distribution maps after isothermal holding at 360 °C ( d ), 400 °C ( e ), 420 °C ( f ); image quality maps combined with phase distribution maps assessed using a deep learning evaluation model after isothermal holding at 360 °C ( g ), 400 °C ( h ), 420 °C ( i ).

The fine, lath-type RA (marked in green) located between BFL stayed stable during final cooling to the room temperature due to higher thermal stability than the blocky RA (Fig.  7 d-f). The fraction of RA measured using the EBSD method ranged from 0.6 to 1.8% in the samples isothermally treated at 420 °C and 400 °C, respectively (Fig.  7 e, f). Despite the high resolution of the EBSD method and reasonable step size applied for measurements (50 nm), the smallest RA laths formed between the BFL cannot be detected because a size of RA laths determined using the TEM method (Fig.  6 ) is in a range from 30 nm to 180 nm. However, such small RA laths are detectable using the XRD method. The differences in RA fractions between EBSD and XRD techniques have been documented in literature 67 , 69 , 71  and are attributed to the spatial resolution limitations of the EBSD method. The XRD results confirmed the tendency observed using the EBSD technique but significantly higher fractions of RA were detected for all heat treatment variants (Table  2 ). The highest fraction of RA of about 10.3 vol% containing 0.77 wt% C was detected in the sample heat treated at 400 °C. An increase in isothermal holding temperature above 400 °C resulted in a decrease both in the fraction of RA and C content in this phase up to 2.8 vol% and 0.65 wt% C, respectively at 440 °C. Due to incomplete bainitic transformation at 420 °C and 440 °C (Fig.  4 b, d) a large fraction of austenite was insufficiently enriched in carbon and as a result transformed into FM during final cooling. The XRD analysis also showed that the RA amount was greater at 400 °C (10.3 vol%) compared to 360 °C (3.4 vol%) and 380 °C (3.6 vol%). It is caused by the prior martensite formation before the isothermal holding step, which limits the amount of austenite available for the transformation into bainite. Typically, without the formation of prior martensite, some higher fraction of RA should be expected at 360 °C and 380 °C 56 , 72 . It was also found that the carbon content in RA increases with decreasing the transformation temperature, starting from 0.65 wt% at 440 °C and reaching 0.98 wt% at 360 °C. Lowering the bainitic transformation temperature resulted in an increase in the driving force for the transformation leading to the formation of a larger fraction of bainite, which finally causes a greater enrichment of carbon in austenite.

sections.heading: Investigation of bainitic ferrite thickness
paragraphs: The calculations (Fig.  8 ) and microstructure observations (Fig.  9 ) together verified a strong correlation between the transformation temperature and the thickness of the BFL. The computational results indicated that carrying out the transformation below 370 °C promotes nanoscale thickness in the BFL. In samples subjected to isothermal holding at 360 °C, the thickness of the BFL approached the border between nano- and submicron scales. When the holding temperature exceeded 360 °C, their thickness progressively increased. Within the 360–400 °C range the BFL showed a minor increase in thickness (107–124 nm), whereas at 440 °C, they experienced some coarsening (165 nm). The relatively wide width range of BFL and austenite laths’ thickness are often found in Al-containing steels 20 , 68 .
Fig. 9 Thickness of bainitic ferrite laths measured using STEM images obtained at isothermal holding temperatures: ( a ) 360 °C, ( b ) 400 °C and ( c ) 440 °C.

The comparison between the calculated and measured values of the BFL thickness showed the partial agreement (Fig.  9 ). At the lowest isothermal holding temperature, the model tends to overestimate the thickness by about 18 nm, whereas at the higher temperatures, the discrepancy was smaller (around 4–6 nm). Consequently, the model for calculating the BFL thickness effectively predicts the possibility of achieving a submicron structure within the selected transformation temperature range.

sections.heading: Influence of different isothermal holding temperature on hardness
paragraphs: Results of hardness measurements reflect the microstructure changes resulting from different applied isothermal holding temperature (Table  2 ). The lowest hardness of 397HV10 was noted for the sample after isothermal holding at 400 °C due to the presence of certain fraction of ductile RA (10.3 vol%, Table  2 ) located between BFL and a very small fraction of MA areas (Fig.  5 c). An increase in isothermal holding temperature above 400 °C resulted in an increase in hardness to about 410HV10 and 405HV10 in samples isothermally treated at 420 °C and 440 °C, respectively. This is due to an increase in the fraction of hard FM (Fig.  7 g-i) and the reduced amount of RA, 6.7 vol% and 2.8 vol% in samples isothermally treated at 420 °C and 440 °C, respectively (Table  2 ). At 420 °C and 440 °C the bainitic transformation was not completed and the enrichment of austenite in carbon was not sufficient to avoid the formation of FM during final cooling to room temperature (Fig.  4 c) and therefore the increased hardness was noted. The formation of prior martensite in samples heat treated below M s  temperature contributed to an increase in hardness to 408HV10 and 417HV10 at 360 °C and 380 °C, respectively compared to the samples treated above M s  temperature. The obtained results are consistent with dilatometric tests and microstructure observations.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Due to their complex nature, bainitic steels are difficult to design, especially for industrial applications and large components, which is commonly the case in the forging industry. For this reason, the kinetics of bainite formation as well as the correlation with resulting microstructures and properties need to be understood in detail. From the investigations on the effect of different isothermal holding temperatures on the above-mentioned features, the following conclusions can be drawn:

A strong effect of prior martensite formation during the cooling to the isothermal holding temperatures on the incubation time is observed, resulting in an acceleration of the bainite formation. An increase of the isothermal holding temperatures in a range above M s  temperature leads to a reduction of the obtainable RA fraction, due to the lower enrichment of carbon during the isothermal holding. Due to the lower stability, more austenite transforms to martensite after isothermal holding. Large variations in microstructure morphology are observed, again in dependency of the heat treatment, including lath-type and coalesced bainite (T iso : 360 °C), as well as fresh martensite (T iso : 420 °C and 440 °C). It is demonstrated that the prediction of the BFL is achieved with the chosen computational model. Regarding the microstructure, isothermal holding at 400 °C is the most beneficial due to its kinetics as well as the stability of RA. The highest fraction of fine lath-type RA (10.3 vol%) and BFL, with a mean thickness of 124 nm, together with a small fraction of martensitic-austenitic areas, were observed at this temperature. Based on these results, heat treatments can be further optimized, potentially enabling the substitution of energy-intensive multi-step heat treatments by single-step processes, contributing to the reduction of the industrial CO 2 -emissions.
